data.title: Dr. Oz urges senators to reject Budd hemp amendment
data.description:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), is urging senators to not support an amendment that would allow a federal ban on most hemp-derived products to take effect in November.

In a Friday letter, Oz noted he had “grave concerns” about the amendment from Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) that would strip from a government funding bill a one-month delay of the ban. 

“Passage of this amendment would undo significant gains that have been made to make clinically-appropriate full-spectrum hemp-derived CBD accessible to the senior citizens and individuals with disabilities that rely on the Medicare program for their healthcare,” the CMS chief wrote. 

The Trump administration earlier this year launched a pilot program that would allow Medicare providers that participate in select programs to offer eligible hemp products to eligible beneficiaries. 

Participants may provide up to $500 worth of hemp products annually. Medicare itself will not reimburse providers for the products, however, so participating organizations bear the costs.  

The administration highlighted the availability of full-spectrum CBD, which contains all of the compounds found in the cannabis plant including trace amounts of THC that are not enough to produce a psychoactive effect. 

But the program encompasses all hemp-derived products containing no more than 0.3 percent delta-9 THC by total weight; the same definition of hemp included in the 2018 Farm Bill. CMS said it would change the requirements if hemp laws changed.  

Oz in the letter said passage of the amendment would “rip away from millions of seniors and disabled Americans the opportunity to benefit from these new programs.” 

The underlying spending bill would also delay the restrictions on intoxicating hemp products enacted last year until December, though cannabinoids that cannot naturally be produced by the cannabis plant would still lose their federal hemp status on November 12. 

Hemp industry stakeholders say the extra month will give them additional time to convince lawmakers that regulation, not prohibition, is the best path forward.   

The provision was inserted into the bill at the behest of the White House, though it has bipartisan backing. Budd’s amendment would strip that delay from the bill.  

Budd and other co-sponsors of the amendment are slowing consideration of the spending bill until they can get a vote. There are currently 13 co-sponsors. 

The senators say they are trying to protect children from illicit products that are intentionally marketed to children.  

The products are labeled as hemp, but contain extremely high levels of synthetic THC, the psychedelic compound in marijuana responsible for a high.   

Oz said the administration shares the same goals and is “focused on preventing dangerous products from reaching Americans.

“You each have my commitment to continue to work with you on meeting our shared goals of ensuring patient access and protection of the public health,” he wrote.

data.title: Live updates: Cassidy will back Blanche's nomination; Senate passes Russia sanctions bill
data.description:
The Senate overwhelmingly passed a bill that will allow for new sanctions on Russia. The legislation, named for its champion, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), passed 86-11.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said Friday morning in a Senate floor speech that he will support acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, likely allowing his nomination to pass the Senate. Cassidy was the final holdout on the nomination.

As the lame duck senator announced his decision, he hesitated, noting he would catch criticism for his decision but assuring his Louisiana constituents that he had thoughtfully considered the vote.

The Senate is scrambling to leave for its August recess but has several hurdles to jump before it gets there after a week of infighting. The biggest items on the list are still to come: Blanche’s nomination for the permanent job and a continuing resolution to fund the government into December.

President Trump on Friday has policy meetings at the White House and a roundtable at the State Department, before heading to Bedminster, N.J.

Follow live here.

data.title: Senate overwhelmingly passes Russia sanctions bill
data.description:
The Senate on Friday passed a long-sought bipartisan bill that would impose harsher sanctions on Russia and the top five buyers of Russian oil, along with extending existing sanctions on Iran. 

That measure was a major legislative goal of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who died suddenly earlier this month. The vote was 86-11.

If enacted, the measure would impose harsher sanctions on Russia and buyers of Russian oil and gas than the U.S. has previously enforced and extend existing sanctions on Iran, aiming to economically squeeze the two countries. The Iran provision was a later add, requested by President Trump, to prevent longstanding sanctions from lapsing at the end of the year.

The bill’s passage underscores an urgency from many lawmakers to make progress in showing support for Ukraine in its war with Russia. Most senators met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last month after he attended Graham’s funeral, and he made the case for more military aid, as well as the sanctions bill.

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) told The Hill last week that the bill is a symbol of Congress’ attitude about the war, but that Trump has a responsibility to further crack down on Russia. 

“Zelensky’s been clear with us; they’re steadily running out of interceptors,” Coons said. “Putin has made it clear he’s going to continue killing civilians and pummeling. And what really matters is not this bill; it’s what does Donald Trump do with it? Will President Trump finally actually take the side of the country that is aligned with our values and our interests and our priorities against the country that isn’t? And we can pass a bill as an important sign that Congress wants him to take more of an active role, but he’s got to decide to do it. That’s what matters.” 

The specifics of the bill caused some friction with Democrats, who generally support Ukraine but were concerned about the power the legislation would give Trump to tariff countries seen as “facilitators” of Russian evasion of sanctions. 

“We’ve seen the ways in which he illegally uses the authorities he has,” Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) told reporters last week. “I think we can write this bill in such a way that we do the necessary work of stopping Putin’s aggression, while at the same time not giving the president even more authorities to handle tariffs in the reckless way in which he is doing it.”

Alexander Bolton contributed reporting.

data.title: Amazon responds to Mamdani's cease-and-desist letter
data.description:
NEW YORK (WPIX) – Amazon has responded to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani‘s cease-and-desist letters that went out to 40 major retailers over the sale of “prohibited motorized scooters and e-bikes.”

Online retailers, including Wayfair, Walmart, Temu, Target and Amazon, were sent cease-and-desist letters demanding that the stores “immediately end the sale of” prohibited scooters and e-bikes to New York City residents and businesses, according to Mamdani.

If not, the stores could face $2,000 fines as of Aug. 18, Mamdani said Wednesday.

Why did Mamdani send cease-and-desist letters?

The prohibited nature of these scooters and e-bikes stems from the fact that some of the retailers’ products exceed the legal speed limits and wattage limits. Some mopeds don’t have proper VINs as well.

The speed limit for e-bikes in New York City is 15 mph. The maximum speed allowance must be under 20 to 25 mph, depending on the bike. Scooters can’t weigh more than 100 pounds or go more than 20 mph.

“Let’s be clear, these are motorcycles being marketed to New Yorkers as bicycles,” said Department of Transportation Commissioner Mike Flynn.

The actions come a week after 17-year-old Gabriel Nacato was fatally struck by an SUV while riding an e-bike in Lower Manhattan. He was on his way from Bensonhurst to fill out summer job applications with a career counselor, Mamdani said.

“The vehicle he was riding is capable of reaching more than 30 miles per hour, a speed that should never be reached in our bike lanes,” Mamdani said.

Amazon responds to Mamdani’s cease-and-desist

A spokesperson for Amazon told Nexstar’s WPIX that the trillion-dollar corporation will be “looking into the products in question” and has no issue working with the mayor and City Council to get it right.

“Safety is a top priority and we require e-bikes sold in our store to meet applicable safety standards and Amazon policies,” the spokesperson said.

Target has yet to respond to WPIX’s request for comment on the matter.

data.title: Trump nominates Project 2025 author to be Interior Department watchdog
data.description:
President Trump has nominated a former White House official and Project 2025 author to be the Interior Department’s internal watchdog, a move that critics say could hurt the integrity of the office’s investigations. 

Trump nominated Dennis Kirk, one of the authors of a chapter of the conservative policy playbook and a former official in the White House Office of Personnel Management during the first Trump administration, to be the department’s inspector general. 

Mark Greenblatt, a former inspector general of the department, recently told The Hill that having someone with clear political leanings in the role of independent watchdog was unprecedented and could hamper investigations and compromise whistleblowers. 

“You have whistleblowers who come to the Office of Inspector General to make complaints, including complaints about senior political officials and sensitive political programs, and their names and identities are supposed to be kept confidential,” said Greenblatt, who was ousted during a Trump administration purge of inspectors general last year. 

“But if you have an administration mole in the office, all of a sudden, does that information become fair game to the administration?” he added. 

This is not Kirk’s first placement within a watchdog’s office. The Washington Post reported that he was also placed inside a watchdog office for the intelligence community last year.

His appointment comes as the Interior Department faces particular scrutiny over Trump’s D.C. projects, specifically the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. 

Recent reports indicate that contracts for work on the pool were issued through an atypical no-bid process. 

Trump and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum have accused “vandals” of damaging the Reflecting Pool, but U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro in the past week moved to drop charges against people accused of damaging it, instead citing a “botched” installation of a coating at the site.

This week, Senate Democrats wrote to the Interior inspector general’s office requesting a probe into the Reflecting Pool saga.

data.title: Francesca Hong fires back at Axelrod over 'zany liberal' criticism
data.description:
Francesca Hong, the leading Democratic candidate in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race, hit back at criticism from Democratic political strategist David Axelrod on Friday. 

Axelrod, who served as the chief strategist for former President Obama’s 2008 and 2012 presidential campaigns, called the democratic socialist a “zany liberal” in a Thursday social media post. 

He suggested Hong’s loss in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary next week would benefit Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race. 

“He is a serious person. She is a font of zany liberal, faculty lounge exotica,” Axelrod said of the two Democratic candidates. 

Hong fired back in a social media post of her own. 

“This tweet is a perfect example of why the consultant class keeps losing elections,” she wrote. “They’re totally clueless, and they’re hellbent on keeping working-class people out of politics.

“I’ve spent more time in kitchens than faculty lounges,” she added. “Perhaps you’d like to come to Wisconsin and work a Friday night dinner rush with me?”

The democratic socialist candidate has faced criticism from Republicans and some within the Democratic Party over her past support for defunding the police and abolishing the Senate and the Supreme Court. 

In an interview with Fox News’s Dana Perino last week, Hong did not renounce her position from social media posts in 2020 that the police should be defunded and said she believes “people can evolve.”

“The governor cannot defund the police, and I won’t defund the police,” Hong said. “But I will invest in the things we know prevent crime. … We have to be tough on causes if we want to prevent crime.” 

Hong is supported by progressive Democrats like California Rep. Ro Khanna and Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar. A chef and former small business owner, the democratic socialist is running on a platform of affordability and universal childcare.

Wisconsin will hold its Democratic primary next Tuesday.

data.title: What's in a foreign-sounding name? Trump's first House primary loss
data.description:
On Tuesday, Michigan’s Democrats served up a string of victories for the left. Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow triumph in the Senate primary may even have raised President Donald Trump hopes about his chances of keeping the chamber. But my favorite subplot of Michigan’s primary night, and surely the result that most surprised Trump, came in the 8th District. Amir Hassan, a candidate Trump had endorsed and rallied with, lost his Republican primary to Thomas Smith, an unknown who had withdrawn in mid-July after mounting basically no campaign and raising basically no money.

“I fell short last night. I make no excuse. It was a tough race,” Hassan said in a video from his car Wednesday morning. Reflecting on his failed endorsement, Trump lamented: “It was a little bit of a person that I thought was a good person — didn’t have much of a chance, but I said: ‘I don’t care. I’m doing it anyway.”

Fundraising cannot explain Hassan’s defeat. He had ample financial backing, though he still raised less than the Democratic nominee. Nor is Trump reviled in the predominantly white 8th District, which backed him for president in 2024 even as it sent a Democrat to Congress. The apparent explanation is that the Republican electorate could not get past Hassan’s Muslim-sounding name.

Hassan, who has described himself as Christian since early in the campaign, is African American and has no Middle Eastern background. The surname proves nothing about its bearer’s religion, as Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) might attest (no relation). Still, even Trump’s stamp of approval failed to sway the race, handing the president his first House-primary endorsement defeat of his second term.

Smith had actually endorsed another candidate. The fact that he won anyway suggests many of his voters had no idea who he was and went simply by the Caucasian vibe of his name.

A foreign-sounding name, Middle Eastern or otherwise, does not invariably spell doom. It did not doom Vivek Ramaswamy, who trounced his Groyper-esque opponent Casey Putsch in Ohio’s gubernatorial primary earlier this year. Ramaswamy, however, entered the race with national celebrity and a vast fortune, both of which improves an electorate’s pronunciation. Tuesday made grim reading for anyone who imagined the Republican base wholesale having moved beyond this sort of crude identitarian reflex.

To some on the right, the result was cause for celebration. “’Amir Hassan’ claims he’s not a Muslim, but it doesn’t matter,” chimed Laura Loomer. “His name sounds like he’s fresh off the boat and MAGA voters reject the Islamic infiltration of our country and party.” If Tuesday offered any indication of the Islamic “takeover” of the Republican Party, as Loomer so often describes it, she and her fellow extremists haven’t much to fear.

It may make especially grim reading for El-Sayed, who now enters the general election against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), whose name is as gloriously generic as “Thomas Smith.” Republicans are already harping on El-Sayed’s proper first name, Abdulrahman, and his bro-fisting with lefty streamer Hasan Piker, who once declared that “America deserved 9/11,” in an effort to reduce El-Sayed to some sort of Islamist caricature. After a bruising primary, El-Sayed must win over Republicans as well as Haley Stevens supporters, some of whom regard him as antisemitic, radical and interested chiefly in Arab and Muslim voters.

El-Sayed’s response is to stick to policy. “Yeah, my name is Abdul. I’ll say the whole thing: Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. And I want you to have health care, because you know what? Chances are, you probably had a doctor you trust with a name like mine,” he told Semafor’s David Weigel in June.

It will nevertheless be far easier for Republicans to persuade Michigan voters that El-Sayed wants to impose socialism-inflected Sharia law than it was for Andrew Cuomo to make the charge stick in New York City against Zohran Mamdani. But it is also possible that El-Sayed can Mamdani his way out of it.

William Liang is a writer living in San Francisco. He volunteers for Connie Chan’s congressional campaign in California’s 11th District.

data.title: Buc-ee's responds as beaver logo battle gains national attention
data.description:
BEAVERCREEK, Ohio (WDTN) – As the lawsuit between Buc-ee’s and Beaver Mini Mart continues, the former is speaking out for the first time.

Arch Aplin III, owner of Buc-ee’s, said the matter could have been avoided altogether.

Huber Heights, Ohio, Mayor Jeff Gore spoke with Aplin about the lawsuit and revealed details from that conversation in a Facebook post.

Gore said that he was told that the owner of Beaver Mini Mart seeks to trademark Beavermart at the federal level. Gore said he was told that this trademark filing was made after Buc-ee’s announced its Huber Heights location.

“Mr Aplin told me directly that Buc-ee’s had no issues with Beavermart using the Beaver logo in Beavercreek. He understood and said that makes sense. What Buc-ee’s did not want was a series of Beavermarts popping up across the state or regionally or eventually nationally that violated their trademark.”

Gore said that Aplin has sent emails and mailings to attempt a resolution but reportedly only recently received a response from the Mini Mart.

The lawsuit between the two entities has become a national headline, as many, including Beavercreek community members and Ohio state leaders, have rallied behind the small business. A GoFundMe for the business has raised over $45,000 as of this publication.

The suit argues that the Mini Mart’s beaver, with its “wide eyes and a smile” that also “uses red as a predominant color,” is too similar to Buc-ee’s and could cause confusion.

This is not the first of such claims from the travel center chain, as it has sued several other businesses state and nationwide.

Bryan Schroll, a legal expert at Cedarville University, said most businesses end up settling and changing their logo.

A cash mob was happening Friday in Beavercreek. The community-hosted event urged residents to buy at least $20 worth of items from the Mini Mart, with organizers saying that it brings back a community tradition.

data.title: Trump touts wins in Tennessee primary despite Ogles loss
data.description:
President Trump touted his endorsement track record Friday after one of his picks, Rep. Andy Ogles (R), lost his Thursday primary in Tennessee.

“Last night was another good night for Endorsements, 8-1, and the 1 was a person who I remained loyal to even though he had virtually no chance of winning, and was running against a Great ‘Trump’ Candidate,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, throwing his support behind Charlie Hatcher, who defeated Ogles to secure the Republican nomination.

Hatcher, a former state agriculture commissioner, was backed by term-limited Gov. Bill Lee (R) ahead of Thursday’s primary for the 5th Congressional District. Ogles, whom Trump held a tele-rally for in late July, has come under scrutiny in recent months for statements about Muslims and homosexuality.

Hatcher’s win on Thursday marks the second loss on the president’s endorsement scorecard this week. In Michigan, Trump-backed Amir Hassan lost his Republican House primary to take on Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.) on Tuesday. Thomas Smith, who dropped out of the race, secured the GOP nod.

Trump’s primary endorsement record has remained largely strong this cycle, though he has notched some high-profile losses in key gubernatorial primaries. His initial picks for governor in Iowa, South Carolina and Georgia all fell short in their respective primaries.

Still, he has secured some key primary wins, successfully helping to oust GOP Sens. John Cornyn (Texas) and Bill Cassidy (La.), along with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), in their contests earlier this cycle.

In Tennessee, Trump notably declined to endorse in the GOP primary for governor. Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn clinched the nomination, beating Republican Rep. John Rose. The president reportedly noted the awkwardness in the race, according to the Nashville Banner, as he had endorsed both in previous elections.

His endorsees in seven of Tennessee’s nine House districts all won their primaries on Thursday. He did not weigh in on the primary to fill Rose’s seat in the 6th Congressional District. GOP state Rep. Johnny Garrett secured the nomination for the solid red seat, defeating former Rep. Van Hilleary (R).

data.title: How the transportation bill can protect communities, wildlife and taxpayers
data.description:
America’s transportation infrastructure is the backbone of the nation’s economy, keeping commuters safe, supply chains moving and essential services accessible. The current surface transportation law, enacted five years ago, plays a critical role in maintaining those functions but is set to expire in September.

The Senate is working on legislation that would extend current transportation programs through early December and provide lawmakers with additional time to work on a surface transportation reauthorization bill. In May, the House took a significant step forward when the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee passed the BUILD America 250 Act with a strong bipartisan vote of 62-2.

The bill’s return on investment will depend in part on whether lawmakers preserve and strengthen several less well-known but highly effective programs: the Wildlife Crossings Program, the Protect program and the National Culvert Removal, Replacement, and Restoration Grant program.

As Congress advances toward a final reauthorization bill, lawmakers across the political spectrum should continue to enhance these programs to ensure that taxpayer dollars are invested in ways that reduce crashes, keep roads open during disasters, and help local economies thrive.

Animal-vehicle collisions are a persistent national public safety problem, resulting in hundreds of human fatalities, more than 26,000 injuries and over $8 billion in annual costs — more than $12 billion when adjusted for inflation. They can disproportionately affect rural communities, where fish, wildlife and livestock are central to the landscape, culture, and traditions.

Wildlife crossings, such as overpasses and underpasses, paired with fencing, are proven solutions that can reduce collisions by up to 97 percent. Fewer collisions mean improved safety for the traveling public, lower medical costs and fewer traffic disruptions. Wildlife crossings can also support livestock activity, such as grazing, while facilitating species movement and migration, enabling access to food, water, and habitat.

The value of wildlife crossings is reflected in robust demand from states, Tribes and local governments for Wildlife Crossings Program funding. Although authorized at $350 million over five years, applicants requested nearly $550 million in the first round alone. More than a dozen states have passed legislation to generate matching funds and compete for federal grants.

Encouragingly, the committee-passed bill would increase funding for wildlife crossings to $400 million over five years, make the program permanent and eliminate the cost-share match requirement for Tribes to help ensure all eligible projects receive fair consideration.

This is meaningful progress, but funding still falls short of growing demand. Congress should increase Wildlife Crossings Program funding to between $100 million and $200 million annually to provide sufficient resources to scale up wildlife crossing projects and planning.

Extreme weather events damage transportation infrastructure and contribute to nearly 6,500 fatal crashes and more than 450,000 injuries each year. The Protect Program helps Americans nationwide proactively reduce disaster risk by strengthening the surface transportation network.

In West Virginia, for example, the program awarded $3 million to reduce flood risk along the main evacuation route for the city of Richwood. In Minnesota, Protect formula funding helped create the state Department of Transportation’s resilience improvement plan, which outlines natural hazard vulnerabilities and response options so planners can systematically reduce future risk from natural hazards.

It’s promising that the BUILD America 250 Act expands funding for the competitive grant portion of the Protect Program, which is essential for driving novel solutions that enhance disaster resilience.

However, the bill would eliminate the formula component that currently provides every state with baseline resilience funding. This means states could no longer count on predictable annual funding at a time when communities face increasingly frequent and costly disasters.

The $7.3 billion in cumulative formula funding from the current surface transportation law gives states stable, flexible resources to direct where needed most. Congress should maintain the balance of Protect formula funding and competitive grants to ensure sustained nonfederal investment in resilient transportation infrastructure.

Roughly 68 million culverts, which allow water and animals to pass under roads across the country, were built using 1950s-era designs. When these outdated structures fail under today’s more intense storms, local economies bear the brunt of washed-out roads and inundated homes, businesses and agricultural lands.

Replacing these structures proactively — before the next storm — is far less costly than emergency repairs. Undersized culverts affect people, fish and wildlife through blocked habitat access, high maintenance costs and damaged road infrastructure.

As reflected in the House bill, Congress should preserve the National Culvert Removal, Replacement, and Restoration Grant at current funding levels to provide the support necessary to undertake upgrades that reduce disaster risk, effectively pass sediment and debris and restore stream functions.

America needs a comprehensive transportation bill that keeps roads open during and after storms, reduces collisions, and helps local economies prosper. The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee’s robust endorsement of the BUILD America 250 Act demonstrates strong bipartisan support for achieving this. 

To get the highest return on investment from the next surface transportation law, Congress must strengthen these Wildlife Crossings Program, the Protect Program and the National Culvert Removal, Replacement, and Restoration Grant in the final bill. Doing so will make Americans safer, wildlife better protected and communities more accessible and prosperous.

Forbes Tompkins works on The Pew Charitable Trusts’ U.S. conservation project; Ian Nakayama is senior government affairs manager at the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership; and Jason Smith is a vice president at Jacobs, a science-based consulting and advisory leader.
